messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Shopowner
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Vignette:
Leilani Makana was sixty-six years old, a divorced shopowner of Pacific Islander descent who had run a small convenience store in her neighborhood for thirty years. The event that shattered her sense of safety happened on a Tuesday evening in late October, just after she had locked up for the night. Two plainclothes officers approached her in the alley behind the store, shouting questions she could not understand, their flashlights blinding her. She remembered raising her hands, the cold metal of a gun pressed against her temple, the gravel scraping her knees as she was forced to the ground. The rest was a blur of pain, shouting, and the smell of asphalt. She had come to believe there were parts of that night she simply could not recall, no matter how hard she tried—gaps that felt like holes in her own history. The memory itself was so extreme that it hardly seemed real; sometimes she sat and stared at her hands and wondered if any of it had actually happened, or if she had dreamed the whole thing. But she could not put it into words. When her daughter asked what occurred, Leilani’s mouth went dry; she shook her head and said, “I can’t tell it.” The story felt trapped somewhere in her body, not in her mind.

In the weeks that followed, Leilani noticed that the time of day the event had happened—just after dusk, when the alley behind the store grew dark—became unbearable. As the sun dipped below the roofline, her chest tightened and her vision dimmed. She began closing the shop an hour earlier, telling herself it was better for business to adjust, but the real reason was that she could not bear being outside after that hour. She also started avoiding any place that was dimly lit; at home she kept every lamp on, even in the daytime, because the shadows reminded her of the flashlights and the sudden sensation of being watched. The feeling of being observed was constant now. In the store, she would glance over her shoulder at customers, certain they were studying her, waiting for her to slip up. Even the security camera above the register felt accusatory. When she felt dizzy—a sensation that came without warning, a lightheaded spin that made her grab the counter—she was sure she was about to collapse, that her body was betraying her. She began to believe that her reactions since the event proved she was a lousy coper, but beneath that was something deeper—a gnawing sense of inadequacy that had no clear origin. She felt fundamentally unequal to the demands of her own life: inadequate as a shopkeeper who could no longer keep her business running the way it always had, inadequate as a mother who could not find the words to explain to her daughter why she was so changed, and inadequate as a person who could not simply snap out of it. What frightened her most was the thought that she was going crazy, that her mind was finally breaking after all these years of running the shop alone.

To manage the constant dread, Leilani developed habits that she knew, somewhere beneath the panic, were not helping. She avoided any mention of the date the event had occurred; when October came around the next year, she threw away the calendar page and refused to open her mail. But the avoidance took a different form as well: she spent money. At first it was small things—a candle, a new teapot—but soon she was buying clothes she never wore, gadgets she did not need, online orders arriving daily at the shop. It was a way to feel something other than fear, a few minutes of focus on the screen instead of on the watching eyes she imagined behind her. She knew the credit card bills were piling up, but the thought of stopping made the dizziness surge, and she would click “buy” again to push it away. The purchases were also a fragile antidote to the inadequacy; for a brief moment, holding a new object in her hands, she felt like someone who could still make choices, who still had control.

The consequence of her avoidance was tangible. Her shop, once a lively hub where neighbors stopped to chat, grew quiet. Leilani rushed customers through their purchases, kept the blinds half-drawn, and stopped stocking the shelves herself because she refused to walk into the back storage room where the light switch clicked with a sound that reminded her of a gun's safety. Her daughter, who had once helped on weekends, stopped coming because Leilani snapped at her when she tried to talk about what happened. The relationship grew brittle, another loss layered onto the trauma, and it only deepened Leilani’s conviction that she was inadequate—unable even to hold on to the people she loved.

What finally brought Leilani to seek help was a morning in late spring when she woke up and could not remember how she had gotten home from the shop the night before. The gap in memory was terrifying, tipping her into the old fear that she was truly losing her mind. She made an appointment at a clinic downtown, not because she hoped to feel better, but because she was afraid of what might happen if she did not. She sat in the waiting room with her hands clasped, her eyes fixed on a clock whose hands were moving inexorably toward the time of day she dreaded most. She was not sure what she wanted—perhaps just for someone to tell her that she was not crazy, that the gaps and the dizziness and the spending and the awful feeling of inadequacy were all part of something she could name. But even that felt too much to hope for.
